parakeet: Now let's talk about assumption three. It assumes disbelief requires a theory of everything. The third hidden assumption is that disbelief requires a theory of everything. This is where we have to expose the unfair standard. Because when Christians ask if you don't believe in God, how do you explain the universe? They're often treating atheism like it has to be a complete explanation of the universe. But that's not what atheism is. Atheism is not the claim that I know how everything began. Atheism is not the claim that I can explain every mystery of the universe. Atheism is not the claim that I've solved cosmology, consciousness, morality, biology, or human purpose. Atheism is the position that the God claim has not met its burden of proof. That's all it is. I don't have to personally explain the entire universe in order to say you have not demonstrated that your God exists. Not knowing the answer to one question does not make someone else's answer true. A gap in knowledge is not proof of theology. And that's the difference between a lack of belief and total explanation. If someone says a dragon lives in my attic, I don't need a complete theory of attic acoustics, insulation patterns, dust movement, air pressure, and neighborhood reptile migration patterns to say, I don't believe you've shown that there's a dragon in your attic. The specifications of the attic are profoundly irrelevant to the conversation in the absence of an actual dragon in the attic. So before we start debating attic insulation, you need to show me the dragon. Before we start debating where the dragon came from, what the dragon eats, whether the dragon exists outside of time, whether the dragon is invisible and material or spiritually discerned, you still need to demonstrate that there is indeed a dragon. The same applies to God. You cannot assert that a God did when you haven't successfully established that a God is. I don't need to know everything about the universe to recognize that your extraordinary claim has not been demonstrated. And this is where apologetics often confuses humility with defeat. If I say I don't know, the apologist hears, aha, so you need God. That's a sleight of hand. Unanswered questions are not religious property, and intellectual humility is not a doorway back into superstition. The honest answer to a mystery is not to pretend that we know. The honest answer is to keep investigating with better tools, better questions, better evidence, and enough humility to admit when we have not reached the answer yet. So no, disbelief doesn't require a theory of everything. Disbelief only requires recognizing that the claim in front of me has not been proven. And if your God claim cannot stand unless I personally solved the universe first, then your argument was never as strong as you thought it was.
